name: Cioteronel

card.summary: Cioteronel is a discontinued topical antiandrogen that was developed to treat male-pattern hair loss and acne by blocking androgen action at the scalp and skin.
card.note: Never marketed; development ended after efficacy fell short.

quick.overview:
Cioteronel (code name CPC-10997) is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen that was investigated as a topical treatment for androgenetic alopecia (male-pattern hair loss) and acne, and as an oral drug for benign prostatic hyperplasia. The idea was to block androgen signalling locally in the scalp so that hair follicles are less affected by it.
It was studied from 1989 to 2001, reaching phase II for hair loss and phase III for acne, but development was discontinued because of poor efficacy. It was never marketed, so it is a historical compound rather than something available to use.
quick.how: It was designed as a topical product applied to the scalp. Since it never reached the market, there is no approved regimen, and it appears in hair-loss discussions mainly as an example of earlier antiandrogen approaches.
quick.risks: It is not an approved drug anywhere. Public information on its safety is limited to the fact that development was abandoned for efficacy reasons.

lead: Cioteronel is an investigational nonsteroidal antiandrogen, also known by the code CPC-10997, with the tentative brand names Cyoctol and X-Andron. It was intended as a topical treatment for androgenetic alopecia and acne, and an oral treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia.[1]

Because androgens drive miniaturisation of scalp follicles in male-pattern hair loss, a topical androgen-receptor antagonist was meant to preserve or regrow hair by acting locally. Development ran from 1989 to 2001, reaching phase II studies for androgenetic alopecia and phase III for acne, and ended because of poor efficacy.[1]
It was never approved or sold, and it is classed as an abandoned drug.[1]

chain: Topical antiandrogen applied to the scalp
Blocks androgen action at the follicle

angle.text: It was developed to reduce the androgen effect on scalp follicles without systemic exposure. Development was stopped before approval.

paras: Intended uses were topical treatment of androgenetic alopecia and acne, and oral treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia.[1]
The compound was studied between 1989 and 2001. It progressed to phase III trials for acne and phase II studies for androgenetic alopecia, and was dropped because of poor efficacy.[1]
Cioteronel has the molecular formula C16H28O2 and a molar mass of about 252.4 g/mol. Its CAS number is 89672-11-7.[1]
No studies exist beyond the registered development phases: phase II for androgenetic alopecia and phase III for acne, discontinued for poor efficacy.[1]
